decks.title: Mole Concept — Part 1: Mole, formulae and chemical equivalents
goals: Calculate moles, molecules and atoms from mass and gas volume at STP
Find empirical and molecular formulae from percentage composition
Calculate equivalent weights of acids, bases, salts and redox agents and relate them to molar mass and valency

slides.heading: Counting by Weighing
slides.body_md: Part 1: atomic and molecular masses, the mole, formulae from analysis, and chemical equivalents.

rows: divide or multiply by molar mass
divide or multiply by equivalent weight

visual.alt: Table of links between mass, moles, particles, volume and equivalents

slides.narration: Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them by weighing. This part builds that bridge. We start with atomic and molecular masses and the mole, then find formulae from percentage composition, and finally meet the ISC idea of chemical equivalents, which links the mass of a substance to its combining power.

slides.heading: Atomic and molecular masses
slides.body_md: The **atomic mass unit** (u) is **one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom**, about $1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg. The atomic mass in the periodic table is the **weighted average** over the isotopes; **molecular mass** is the sum of atomic masses in the molecule.

visual.alt: Table of neon isotopes, their masses and abundances, with the weighted average atomic mass

slides.narration: The atomic mass unit is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a carbon twelve atom. The atomic mass listed for an element is an average, weighted by how common each isotope is. Neon is mostly neon twenty, with a little neon twenty two, and the weighted average comes to about twenty point one eight. Molecular mass is simply the sum of the atomic masses in a molecule.

slides.heading: The mole, Avogadro constant and molar volume
slides.body_md: One **mole** contains $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ elementary entities (as many as in 12 g of carbon-12). **Molar mass** in g mol⁻¹ equals the molecular mass in u. At **STP** (273 K, 1 atm) one mole of any gas occupies **22.4 L**.

visual.caption: Worked values are for 0.50 mol of carbon dioxide.

slides.narration: Amount in moles sits at the centre. Multiply by molar mass to get grams. Multiply by the Avogadro constant to get the number of particles. Multiply by twenty two point four litres to get the volume of a gas at standard temperature and pressure. And moles divided by molarity gives the volume of a solution. Whatever you are given, convert to moles first.

slides.heading: Worked example: mole conversions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) For 5.50 g of ammonia ($\ce{NH3}$, $M = 17$ g mol⁻¹) find the amount, the number of molecules and the number of hydrogen atoms. (b) Find the volume at STP of 8.80 g of carbon dioxide ($M = 44$ g mol⁻¹).

**(a)** $n = 5.50/17 = 0.324$ mol. Molecules $= 0.324 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.95 \times 10^{23}$. Hydrogen atoms $= 3 \times 1.95 \times 10^{23} = 5.84 \times 10^{23}$.

**(b)** $n = 8.80/44 = 0.200$ mol; $V = 0.200 \times 22.4 = 4.48$ L.

visual.alt: Table of the mole conversions for ammonia and carbon dioxide samples

slides.narration: Both parts start by finding moles. For ammonia, divide five point five grams by seventeen to get about zero point three two four mole. Multiply by the Avogadro constant for molecules, then by three for hydrogen atoms. For carbon dioxide, eight point eight grams is exactly zero point two mole, and that many moles of any gas at standard conditions fills four point four eight litres.

slides.heading: Quick check: moles and atoms
slides.body_md: Convert a mass of an acid to the number of atoms of one element.
slides.narration: Quick check. First convert the mass to moles of molecules using the molar mass. Then multiply by the Avogadro constant, and finally multiply by the number of atoms of the element in one molecule. Do all three steps before looking at the options.

slides.heading: Percentage composition and empirical formula
slides.body_md: **Mass percent of an element** $=\dfrac{\text{mass of the element in one mole}}{\text{molar mass}} \times 100$. The **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the **molecular formula** is $n \times$ the empirical formula with $n = M / M_\text{empirical}$.

visual.alt: Flow from percentage composition to empirical and molecular formula

slides.narration: To find a formula from analysis, treat the percentages as grams in a hundred gram sample. Divide each by its atomic mass to get moles, then divide all by the smallest to get a ratio. If a ratio is near one point five, multiply everything by two; near one point three three, multiply by three. The molecular formula is a whole number multiple of the empirical formula.

slides.heading: Worked example: empirical formula
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A compound contains 32.4 % sodium, 22.5 % sulfur and 45.1 % oxygen (Na = 23, S = 32, O = 16). Find its empirical formula.

Moles in 100 g: Na $= 32.4/23 = 1.409$; S $= 22.5/32 = 0.703$; O $= 45.1/16 = 2.819$.

Dividing by 0.703: Na : S : O $= 2.00 : 1 : 4.01 \approx 2 : 1 : 4$. Empirical formula: $\ce{Na2SO4}$.

visual.alt: Table of the mole calculation for the empirical formula of sodium sulfate

slides.narration: Treat the percentages as grams in a hundred gram sample and divide by the atomic masses. This gives about one point four moles of sodium, point seven moles of sulfur and two point eight moles of oxygen. Divide all three by the smallest, point seven, and the ratio is two to one to four. The empirical formula is therefore sodium sulfate.

slides.heading: Worked example: molecular formula
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An oxide of nitrogen contains 30.4 % nitrogen and 69.6 % oxygen and has a molar mass of 92 g mol⁻¹. Find the molecular formula.

Moles: N $= 30.4/14 = 2.171$; O $= 69.6/16 = 4.350$. Ratio $1 : 2.00$, so the empirical formula is $\ce{NO2}$ (mass 46).

$n = 92/46 = 2$, so the molecular formula is $(\ce{NO2})_2 = \ce{N2O4}$.

visual.alt: Table of steps from percentage composition to the molecular formula of dinitrogen tetroxide

slides.narration: Moles of nitrogen and oxygen come out in the ratio one to two, giving the empirical formula with one nitrogen and two oxygen atoms, whose formula mass is forty six. The molar mass given is ninety two, exactly twice that, so every subscript doubles and the molecular formula is dinitrogen tetroxide.

slides.heading: Quick check: empirical formula
slides.body_md: Find an empirical formula from percentage composition.
slides.narration: Quick check. Treat the percentages as grams, divide by atomic masses, then divide by the smallest number of moles. Round only when the ratios are very close to whole numbers, and multiply up if you see a fraction such as one point five.

slides.heading: Chemical equivalents
slides.body_md: The **equivalent weight** $E$ is the mass that combines with or displaces 1 part of hydrogen (8 parts of oxygen); in grams it is the **gram equivalent weight**. In general $E = M / n$ where $n$ is the **n-factor**.

rows: electrons gained or lost per formula unit

visual.alt: Table of n-factors and equivalent weights for elements, acids, bases, salts and redox agents

slides.narration: The equivalent weight of a substance is the mass that combines with or replaces one part of hydrogen. It is found by dividing the molar mass by the n factor. For an acid the n factor is its basicity, for a base its acidity, for a salt the total positive charge, and for an oxidising or reducing agent the number of electrons gained or lost per formula unit.

slides.heading: Molar mass versus equivalent weight
slides.body_md: The same molar mass can give different equivalent weights: $E = M / n$ is **never larger** than $M$.

visual.caption: Equivalent weight is the molar mass divided by the n-factor.

slides.narration: Compare the grey and coloured bars. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide have an n factor of one, so equivalent weight equals molar mass. Sulfuric acid and calcium hydroxide have an n factor of two, which halves it. Phosphoric acid fully neutralised has three, and permanganate in acid solution gains five electrons, so its equivalent weight is just over thirty one.

slides.heading: Variable equivalent weight and gram equivalents
slides.body_md: The n-factor depends on the **reaction**, so some substances have **variable equivalent weight**. The **number of gram equivalents** $=\dfrac{\text{mass}}{E}$. For an element, $E = \dfrac{\text{atomic mass}}{\text{valency}}$, so valency $= \dfrac{\text{atomic mass}}{E}$.

visual.alt: Table of variable equivalent weights of phosphoric acid, potassium permanganate and iron

slides.narration: Because the n factor depends on the reaction, one substance can have several equivalent weights. Phosphoric acid can lose one, two or three hydrogen ions. Permanganate gains five, three or one electrons in acidic, neutral and alkaline media. Iron has different valencies in its two chlorides. The number of gram equivalents is the mass divided by the equivalent weight.

slides.heading: Worked example: equivalent weights
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the equivalent weight of (a) oxalic acid dihydrate, $\ce{H2C2O4.2H2O}$ (M = 126), as an acid; (b) magnesium hydroxide (M = 58); (c) iron(III) chloride (M = 162.5) as a salt; (d) copper in $\ce{CuSO4}$ (Cu = 63.5).

**(a)** Dibasic: $126/2 = 63$.  **(b)** Diacidic: $58/2 = 29$.

**(c)** Total positive charge $= 3$: $162.5/3 = 54.2$.  **(d)** Valency 2: $63.5/2 = 31.75$.

visual.alt: Table of four equivalent weight calculations with their n-factors

slides.narration: Each answer is the molar mass divided by the right n factor. Oxalic acid has two replaceable hydrogens, so one hundred twenty six becomes sixty three. Magnesium hydroxide has two hydroxide groups. Iron chloride, as a salt, has a total positive charge of three. And copper has valency two. Always ask first what the n factor is in the reaction concerned.

slides.heading: Worked example: gram equivalents and valency
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) How many gram equivalents are in 7.4 g of $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$ (E = 37)? (b) How many in 10.6 g of $\ce{Na2CO3}$ (E = 53)? (c) A trivalent metal has equivalent weight 9.0. Find its atomic mass.

**(a)** $7.4/37 = 0.20$.  **(b)** $10.6/53 = 0.20$.

**(c)** Atomic mass $= E \times \text{valency} = 9.0 \times 3 = 27$ (aluminium).

visual.alt: Table of gram equivalents of two compounds and the atomic mass of a trivalent metal

slides.narration: Gram equivalents are mass divided by equivalent weight. Seven point four grams of calcium hydroxide and ten point six grams of sodium carbonate both come to point two gram equivalents, although their masses and moles differ. For an element, atomic mass equals equivalent weight times valency, so a trivalent metal of equivalent weight nine has an atomic mass of twenty seven.

slides.heading: Quick check: equivalent weight
slides.body_md: Decide the n-factor for a given reaction.
slides.narration: Quick check. Read the balanced equation to see how many hydrogen ions are actually replaced, because that number is the n factor. Then divide the molar mass by it. Remember that the same acid can have a different equivalent weight in a different reaction.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Atomic mass unit = 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom; average atomic mass is weighted by abundance.
1 mol = $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ entities; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L.
Empirical formula from moles ratio; molecular formula = n × empirical.
E = M / n-factor; gram equivalents = mass / E.
Equivalent weight can vary with the reaction (H₃PO₄, KMnO₄, Fe).

visual.alt: Summary table of tools for Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The atomic mass unit is a twelfth of a carbon twelve atom. A mole holds the Avogadro number of particles and a mole of gas fills twenty two point four litres at standard conditions. Mole ratios give empirical formulae. And equivalent weight is molar mass divided by the n factor, which can change with the reaction.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Always convert to moles first; write the molar mass you use.
Count atoms of an element: moles × atoms per molecule × N_A.
Multiply a ratio of 1.5 by 2 and 1.33 by 3 before writing the formula.
State the n-factor and the reaction when giving an equivalent weight.
Equivalent weight of KMnO₄ and H₃PO₄ depends on the medium or the reaction.

rows: Using M as the equivalent weight of every acid

visual.alt: Table of common slips from Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips for Part 1. Convert to moles first and write down the molar mass. When counting atoms, remember to multiply by the number of atoms in one molecule. Clear fractional ratios by multiplying, not by rounding. And when you quote an equivalent weight, say which n factor you used, because it depends on the reaction.

decks.title: Mole Concept — Part 2: Concentration and stoichiometry
goals: Express concentration as w/w, w/v, molarity, molality, normality and mole fraction and convert between them
Use N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ and M₁V₁ = M₂V₂
Do mass-mass, mass-volume and volume-volume calculations and identify the limiting reagent

slides.heading: Concentration and Stoichiometry
slides.body_md: Part 2: how much solute is in a solution, how solutions react, and how much product a reaction gives.

visual.alt: Table of concentration terms and what each divides by

slides.narration: This part answers two practical questions. How much solute is dissolved in a solution, and how much product does a reaction give. We meet six ways of stating concentration, the equations that make titrations and dilutions easy, and then use balanced equations to calculate masses and volumes and to find the limiting reagent.

slides.heading: Concentration terms
slides.body_md: Percent w/w uses mass of solution; percent w/v uses volume of solution in mL; **molarity** and **normality** use litres of solution; **molality** uses kilograms of solvent; **mole fraction** uses total moles.

visual.alt: Table of the six concentration terms with their definitions

slides.narration: Percent weight by weight divides by the mass of the solution; percent weight by volume divides by the volume in millilitres. Molarity and normality divide by litres of solution. Molality divides by kilograms of solvent, and mole fraction compares moles of one component with the total. Normality equals molarity multiplied by the n factor.

slides.heading: What goes in the denominator
slides.body_md: Always check the denominator: **solution or solvent**, **litres or kilograms**. Molality and mole fraction do not change with temperature; molarity and normality do.

slides.narration: Look at the denominators. Molarity and normality use the volume of the whole solution, so they change when the solution expands on heating. Molality uses the mass of the solvent and mole fraction uses moles, so they do not depend on temperature. Most mistakes in these problems come from using the wrong denominator.

slides.heading: Worked example: molality, mole fraction and molarity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 18.0 g of glucose ($M = 180$ g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in 250 g of water; the solution has density 1.04 g mL⁻¹. Find the molality, mole fraction of glucose and molarity.

$n(\text{glucose}) = 18.0/180 = 0.100$ mol.

**Molality** $= 0.100/0.250 = 0.400$ mol kg⁻¹.

**Mole fraction:** $n(\ce{H2O}) = 250/18 = 13.89$ mol, so $x = 0.100/(0.100 + 13.89) = 0.00715$.

**Molarity:** solution mass $= 268$ g, volume $= 268/1.04 = 257.7$ mL, so $c = 0.100/0.2577 = 0.388$ mol L⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of molality, mole fraction and molarity of the glucose solution

slides.narration: One solution gives three different numbers because each term uses a different reference. For molality divide the point one mole of glucose by the point two five kilograms of water. For mole fraction, find the moles of water as well. For molarity, use the density to find the volume of the whole solution, about two hundred fifty eight millilitres, and divide.

slides.narration: Normality equals molarity multiplied by the n factor. In a titration, the acid and base react in equal numbers of gram equivalents at the end point. Gram equivalents are normality times volume, so the normality of the acid times its volume equals the normality of the base times its volume. When you dilute a solution, molarity times volume stays constant.

slides.heading: Worked example: neutralisation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 20.0 mL of 0.0600 M sulfuric acid neutralises 24.0 mL of sodium hydroxide solution. Find the normality, molarity and strength (g L⁻¹) of the base (NaOH $= 40$ g mol⁻¹).

$N_\text{acid} = 0.0600 \times 2 = 0.120$ N.

$N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$: $0.120 \times 20.0 = N_2 \times 24.0$, so $N_2 = 0.100$ N.

NaOH has n-factor 1, so $M = 0.100$ M and strength $= 0.100 \times 40 = 4.00$ g L⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of normality, volume and milli-equivalents of the acid and base in the neutralisation

slides.narration: First convert the molarity of the acid to normality: point zero six zero molar sulfuric acid is point one two zero normal. Apply the normality equation: point one two zero times twenty equals the unknown times twenty four, giving point one zero zero normal. Sodium hydroxide has an n factor of one, so its molarity is the same, and its strength is four grams per litre.

slides.heading: Quick check: concentration
slides.body_md: Calculate a molality from the mass of solute and solvent.
slides.narration: Quick check. Molality divides moles of solute by the mass of the solvent in kilograms, not by the mass of the whole solution or the volume. Convert the grams of solute to moles, convert grams of water to kilograms, and then divide.

slides.heading: Worked example: concentrated acid label and dilution
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Concentrated nitric acid is labelled 70 % w/w with density 1.41 g mL⁻¹ ($\ce{HNO3}$, $M = 63$). Find its molarity and normality, and the volume needed to make 500 mL of 0.500 M acid.

In 100 g: 70 g $\ce{HNO3}$ $= 1.111$ mol; volume $= 100/1.41 = 70.9$ mL. $c = 1.111/0.0709 = 15.7$ M, or $c = 10 \times 70 \times 1.41/63 = 15.7$ M. The n-factor is 1, so $N = 15.7$ N.

$M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$: $V_1 = 0.500 \times 500/15.67 = 16.0$ mL.

rows: Stock volume for 500 mL of 0.500 M

visual.alt: Table of the steps from the label of nitric acid to the dilution volume

slides.narration: Take a hundred grams of the acid. Seventy grams is nitric acid, about one point one one moles, and the hundred grams occupy about seventy one millilitres. Dividing gives about fifteen point seven molar, and because the n factor is one, the normality is the same. To dilute to half a molar in five hundred millilitres, you need about sixteen millilitres of the stock.

slides.heading: Stoichiometry: mass, volume and moles
slides.body_md: A balanced equation gives **mole ratios**, and at the same T and P, **volume ratios** for gases. Every calculation goes **through moles**.

nodes.label: Mass of A (÷ M) or volume of gas A (÷ 22.4 L)
Moles of B from the coefficient ratio
Mass of B (× M) or gas volume of B (× 22.4 L)

visual.alt: Flow for mass-mass, mass-volume and volume-volume stoichiometry

slides.narration: A balanced equation tells us how many moles of each substance take part. For mass to mass problems, convert the given mass to moles, use the coefficient ratio to get moles of the wanted substance, and convert back to mass. For gases at standard conditions use twenty two point four litres per mole, and for gases at the same temperature and pressure volume ratios equal mole ratios.

slides.heading: Worked example: mass to volume
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 6.0 g of magnesium reacts with excess dilute sulfuric acid: $\ce{Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2}$ (Mg = 24, MgSO₄ = 120). Find the volume of hydrogen at STP and the mass of magnesium sulfate formed.

$n(\ce{Mg}) = 6.0/24 = 0.25$ mol; 1 mol Mg gives 1 mol $\ce{H2}$ and 1 mol $\ce{MgSO4}$.

$V(\ce{H2}) = 0.25 \times 22.4 = 5.6$ L; $m(\ce{MgSO4}) = 0.25 \times 120 = 30.0$ g.

visual.alt: Table of moles and quantities for magnesium, hydrogen and magnesium sulfate

slides.narration: Six grams of magnesium is a quarter of a mole. The balanced equation shows one to one ratios, so a quarter mole of hydrogen and a quarter mole of magnesium sulfate form. A quarter mole of hydrogen at standard conditions is five point six litres, and a quarter mole of magnesium sulfate weighs thirty grams.

slides.heading: Quick check: stoichiometry
slides.body_md: Work backwards from a gas volume to a mass of reactant.
slides.narration: Quick check. Here you are given a gas volume and asked for the mass of a solid reactant. Convert the volume to moles by dividing by twenty two point four litres, use the coefficient ratio from the equation, and then multiply the moles of the solid by its molar mass.

slides.heading: Worked example: mass to mass and volume
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: $\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$ ($\ce{H2O2}$ $= 34$ g mol⁻¹). From 6.8 g of hydrogen peroxide find the mass and the STP volume of oxygen.

$n(\ce{H2O2}) = 6.8/34 = 0.20$ mol, so $n(\ce{O2}) = 0.20 \times 1/2 = 0.10$ mol.

$m(\ce{O2}) = 0.10 \times 32 = 3.2$ g and $V = 0.10 \times 22.4 = 2.24$ L.

visual.alt: Table of steps for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide

slides.narration: Six point eight grams of hydrogen peroxide is point two mole. The equation gives one mole of oxygen for every two moles of peroxide, so point one mole of oxygen forms. That is three point two grams, or two point two four litres at standard conditions. The coefficient ratio is the only link between the two substances.

slides.heading: Limiting reagent
slides.body_md: The **limiting reagent** is used up first. Divide each amount in moles by its coefficient; the **smaller** quotient is limiting. The product and the leftover of the other reagent are calculated from it.

slides.narration: Zero point four mole of aluminium meets zero point three mole of chlorine in the ratio two to three. Divide each by its coefficient: aluminium gives point two, chlorine gives point one. Chlorine is smaller, so chlorine runs out first and decides how much product forms. Zero point two mole of aluminium is left, and zero point two mole of aluminium chloride forms.

slides.heading: Worked example: limiting reagent
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 10.8 g of aluminium reacts with 21.3 g of chlorine: $\ce{2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3}$ (Al = 27, Cl = 35.5). Find the limiting reagent, the mass of aluminium chloride formed and the mass of excess reagent left.

$n(\ce{Al}) = 10.8/27 = 0.400$ mol; $n(\ce{Cl2}) = 21.3/71 = 0.300$ mol. Moles ÷ coefficient: Al $0.200$, $\ce{Cl2}$ $0.100$, so chlorine is limiting.

$n(\ce{AlCl3}) = 0.300 \times 2/3 = 0.200$ mol, $m = 0.200 \times 133.5 = 26.7$ g. Al used $= 0.200$ mol, so Al left $= 0.200 \times 27 = 5.4$ g.

visual.alt: Table of amounts before and after the reaction of aluminium with chlorine

slides.narration: Find the moles of each reactant, divide by the coefficients and compare. Chlorine gives the smaller number, so it is limiting. All the product is calculated from chlorine: point two mole of aluminium chloride, which is twenty six point seven grams. The aluminium that did not react is the difference, point two mole or five point four grams.

slides.heading: Quick check: limiting reagent
slides.body_md: Identify the limiting reagent and the mass of product.
slides.narration: Quick check. Convert both reactant masses to moles, divide each by its coefficient in the balanced equation, and see which is smaller. That reagent decides the amount of product, so use its moles, not the other reagent, to find the mass formed.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Molarity and normality use litres of solution; molality uses kg of solvent; mole fraction uses total moles.
N = M × n-factor; N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ at a neutralisation end point; M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ on dilution.
From a label: M = 10 × (percent w/w) × density / M(solute).
Stoichiometry: mass → moles → coefficient ratio → moles → mass or volume.
Limiting reagent: smallest (moles ÷ coefficient).

visual.alt: Summary table of tools for Part 2

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Choose the right denominator for each concentration term. Normality is molarity times the n factor, and at a neutralisation end point normality times volume is equal on both sides. Stoichiometry always goes through moles and the coefficient ratio. Finally, the limiting reagent, the one with the smallest moles divided by coefficient, decides how much product forms.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Write the balanced equation first and check the coefficients.
Convert mL to L before dividing for molarity or normality.
Use the limiting reagent, never the excess one, for the yield.
In the normality equation use the same volume unit on both sides.
State the n-factor when converting between molarity and normality.

visual.alt: Table of common slips from Part 2 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips for Part 2. Always begin with a balanced equation. Convert millilitres to litres before dividing. Use the limiting reagent for the product and subtract to find the excess left. Keep the volume units the same on both sides of the normality equation, and always state the n factor when you convert between molarity and normality.

sections.body_md:
**1 u** $= \tfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of a carbon-12 atom $\approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27}$ kg. **Average atomic mass** $= \sum(\text{fractional abundance} \times \text{isotopic mass})$. **Molecular mass** is the sum of atomic masses of the atoms in the molecule.

**Mole:** the amount of substance containing $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ elementary entities, as many as in 12 g of carbon-12 (the Avogadro constant $N_\text{A}$). **Molar mass** (g mol⁻¹) equals the molecular mass in u. At **STP** (273 K, 1 atm) one mole of any gas occupies **22.4 L** (gram molecular volume). Molar mass of a gas $= \text{density at STP} \times 22.4$.

sections.heading: 2. Percentage composition, empirical and molecular formulae
sections.body_md:
**Mass percent of an element** $= \dfrac{\text{mass of the element in one mole}}{\text{molar mass}} \times 100$.

**Empirical formula:** take the percentages as grams in 100 g; divide each by the atomic mass to get moles; divide by the smallest; multiply all by 2, 3 … if a ratio is near 1.5 or 1.33. **Molecular formula** $= (\text{empirical formula})_n$ with $n = M / M_\text{empirical}$. For a hydrate $\ce{MX.xH2O}$, $x = n(\ce{H2O}) / n(\text{anhydrous salt})$. Vapour density $= M / 2$.

key_terms.definition_md: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
Density of a gas relative to hydrogen; M = 2 × vapour density.

sections.heading: 4. Variable equivalent weight and gram equivalents
sections.body_md:
The n-factor depends on the reaction, so some substances have **variable equivalent weight**:

- $\ce{H3PO4}$ ($M = 98$): $E = 98.0, 49.0, 32.7$ g eq⁻¹ when one, two or three H⁺ are replaced.
- $\ce{KMnO4}$ ($M = 158$): $E = 31.6$ (acidic, $\ce{Mn^2+}$, $n = 5$), $52.7$ (neutral, $\ce{MnO2}$, $n = 3$), $158$ (alkaline, manganate, $n = 1$).
- Iron: $E = 56/2 = 28$ in iron(II) salts and $56/3 = 18.7$ in iron(III) salts.

**Number of gram equivalents** $= m / E$. For an element, valency $= \text{atomic mass}/E$. Equal gram equivalents of substances react with each other. *Experimental determination of equivalent weights is not required.*

key_terms.definition_md: Different equivalent weights of one substance in different reactions or media.
Combining power of an element; atomic mass divided by equivalent weight.

sections.heading: 5. Concentration terms and the volumetric equations
sections.body_md:
**Percent w/w** $= \dfrac{\text{g solute}}{\text{g solution}} \times 100$; **percent w/v** $= \dfrac{\text{g solute}}{\text{mL solution}} \times 100$; **molarity** $M = n/V(\text{L})$; **molality** $m = n/\text{kg solvent}$; **normality** $N = \text{gram equivalents}/V(\text{L}) = M \times n\text{-factor}$; **mole fraction** $x_\text{A} = n_\text{A}/\sum n$ (the sum of all mole fractions is 1).

Molarity and normality depend on temperature (volume); molality and mole fraction do not. **From a label:** $M = \dfrac{10 \times (\%\ \text{w/w}) \times \rho}{M_\text{solute}}$ with $\rho$ in g mL⁻¹. **Neutralisation:** $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$. **Dilution:** $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$. **Mixing:** $M = \dfrac{M_1V_1 + M_2V_2}{V_1 + V_2}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Moles of solute per litre of solution.
Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.
Gram equivalents of solute per litre of solution.
Moles of one component divided by total moles.

sections.heading: 6. Stoichiometry and the limiting reagent
sections.body_md:
A balanced equation gives **mole ratios** (and volume ratios for gases at the same temperature and pressure). **Plan:** mass $\to$ moles ($\div M$), or gas volume at STP $\to$ moles ($\div 22.4$ L); then the coefficient ratio; then moles $\to$ mass ($\times M$) or volume ($\times 22.4$ L).

**Limiting reagent:** divide each amount in moles by its coefficient; the smallest quotient identifies the reagent that is used up first. Product is calculated from the limiting reagent only; the excess reagent left $= $ initial moles $-$ moles used.

key_terms.definition_md: The quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced equation.
The reactant used up first, which limits the amount of product.
The reactant left over when the limiting reagent is exhausted.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Counting molecules instead of atoms, or forgetting the atoms per molecule.
- Rounding a ratio such as 1.5 or 1.33 instead of multiplying to clear it.
- Taking the equivalent weight of every acid as M/2, or ignoring that it depends on the reaction or medium.
- Using mL instead of L when calculating molarity or normality.
- Using the mass of solution (instead of solvent) for molality.
- Calculating the yield from the excess reagent instead of the limiting reagent.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a definition, a molar mass or a single conversion.
- Formula determination: moles (1), ratio (1), empirical and molecular formula (1).
- Equivalent weight: the n-factor stated (½), E = M/n with the answer (1).
- Titration or concentration numericals: formula (1), substitution with units (1), answer with unit (1).
- Limiting reagent: identification with the moles ÷ coefficient comparison (1–2), product and excess (1–2).

cards.front_md: Definition of the atomic mass unit?
cards.back_md: One twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (about 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).

cards.front_md: Why is the atomic mass of chlorine 35.5 u?
cards.back_md: It is the abundance-weighted average of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

cards.front_md: Avogadro constant?
One mole of a gas at STP occupies?
How do you find the molar mass of a gas from its density at STP?
cards.back_md: M = density (g L⁻¹) × 22.4 L mol⁻¹.

cards.front_md: Number of atoms in n moles of a molecule with a atoms each?
cards.back_md: $n \times a \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}$

cards.front_md: Relation of vapour density to molar mass?
cards.back_md: Molar mass = 2 × vapour density.

cards.front_md: Mass percent of an element in a compound?
cards.back_md: Mass of the element in one mole ÷ molar mass × 100.

cards.front_md: Steps to find an empirical formula?
cards.back_md: Percent → grams in 100 g → moles → divide by the smallest → clear fractions.

cards.front_md: A mole ratio of 1 : 1.5 means multiply by?
cards.back_md: 2 (giving 2 : 3).

cards.front_md: A mole ratio of 1 : 1.33 means multiply by?
cards.back_md: 3 (giving 3 : 4).

cards.front_md: Relation between molecular and empirical formulae?
cards.back_md: Molecular formula = (empirical formula)ₙ with n = M ÷ empirical formula mass.

cards.front_md: Empirical formula of ethene and propene?
cards.back_md: CH₂ for both.

cards.front_md: How to find x in CuSO₄·xH₂O from heating data?
cards.back_md: x = moles of water lost ÷ moles of anhydrous salt left.

cards.front_md: Definition of equivalent weight?
cards.back_md: Mass that combines with or displaces 1 part of hydrogen (8 of oxygen, 35.5 of chlorine).

cards.front_md: General formula for equivalent weight?
cards.back_md: E = molar mass ÷ n-factor.

cards.front_md: n-factor of an acid and of a base?
cards.back_md: Basicity (H⁺ replaced) for an acid; acidity (OH⁻ replaced) for a base.

cards.front_md: Equivalent weight of a salt?
cards.back_md: Molar mass ÷ total positive (or negative) charge, e.g. Al₂(SO₄)₃: 342 ÷ 6 = 57.

cards.front_md: Equivalent weight of an oxidising or reducing agent?
cards.back_md: Molar mass ÷ electrons gained or lost per formula unit.

cards.front_md: Equivalent weight of H₂SO₄?
Equivalent weights of H₃PO₄ in the three neutralisations?
cards.back_md: 98.0, 49.0 and 32.7 g eq⁻¹ (one, two, three H⁺ replaced).

cards.front_md: Equivalent weights of KMnO₄ in acidic, neutral, alkaline media?
Valency from equivalent weight?
cards.back_md: Valency = atomic mass ÷ equivalent weight.

cards.front_md: Number of gram equivalents?
cards.back_md: Mass ÷ equivalent weight.

cards.front_md: Molarity versus molality?
cards.back_md: Molarity: mol per litre of solution. Molality: mol per kg of solvent.

cards.front_md: Relation between normality and molarity?
cards.back_md: N = M × n-factor.

cards.front_md: Which concentration terms are independent of temperature?
cards.back_md: Molality and mole fraction (percent w/w too); molarity and normality are not.

cards.front_md: Normality and molarity equations?
cards.back_md: N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ (neutralisation); M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ (dilution).

cards.front_md: Molarity from a label?
cards.back_md: M = 10 × percent w/w × density (g mL⁻¹) ÷ molar mass.

cards.front_md: Mole fraction of A?
cards.back_md: nA ÷ (nA + nB); all mole fractions add up to 1.

cards.front_md: Plan for any stoichiometry problem?
cards.back_md: Convert to moles, use the coefficient ratio, convert to the wanted unit.

cards.front_md: How to find the limiting reagent?
cards.back_md: Moles ÷ coefficient for each reactant; the smallest identifies it.

questions.stem_md: A pharmacist weighs out 4.90 g of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄ (molar mass 98 g mol⁻¹), for a laboratory reagent. The number of oxygen atoms in this sample is closest to:
questions.solution_md: $n = 4.9 / 98 = 0.05$ mol of molecules, and each molecule has 4 oxygen atoms, so the atoms are $0.05 \times 4 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.20 \times 10^{23}$ — option (a). (b) counts molecules only; (c) is ten times too large.

questions.stem_md: Natural lithium is 7.5 % lithium-6 (isotopic mass 6.015 u) and 92.5 % lithium-7 (isotopic mass 7.016 u). Its average atomic mass is:
questions.solution_md: Average mass $= 0.075 \times 6.015 + 0.925 \times 7.016 = 6.941 \approx 6.94$ u — option (b). (a) is the simple mean of 6.015 and 7.016, which ignores the abundances.

questions.stem_md: A sample of sulfur dioxide gas (molar mass 64 g mol⁻¹) collected from a furnace flue has a mass of 6.4 g. Taking the molar volume as 22.4 L at STP, its volume at STP is:
questions.solution_md: $n = 6.4 / 64 = 0.1$ mol, so $V = 0.1 \times 22.4 = 2.24$ L — option (a). (b) is the volume of one whole mole.

questions.stem_md: The atomic mass unit, u, is defined as:

options.text_md: the mass of one hydrogen atom
one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
one twelfth of the average mass of a carbon atom of natural carbon
the mass of one proton plus one electron

questions.solution_md: By definition 1 u is exactly one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (about 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) — option (b). The mass of a hydrogen atom is close to, but not exactly, 1 u, and natural carbon contains some carbon-13.

questions.stem_md: Four samples are prepared in a school laboratory. Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms?

options.text_md: 11.2 L of ammonia, NH₃, at STP

questions.solution_md: Atoms in units of $N_\text{A}$: methane $1 \times 5 = 5$; water $2 \times 3 = 6$; neon $1 \times 1 = 1$; ammonia $0.5 \times 4 = 2$. Water has the most — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L at STP, whether the gas is hydrogen or chlorine.

**Reason (R):** Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the molar volume is the same for all (ideal) gases at STP. R is Avogadro’s law, which is exactly why one mole (a fixed number of molecules) occupies the same volume — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The relative atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5.

**Reason (R):** Every chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5 u.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: 35.5 is the weighted average of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 over their natural abundances. R is false: individual atoms have masses of about 35 u or 37 u; no single atom weighs 35.5 u — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? One mole of hydrogen gas occupies only 11.2 L at STP, because hydrogen is the lightest of all gases.
questions.solution_md: False. One mole of any ideal gas, including hydrogen, occupies 22.4 L at STP. The molar volume depends on temperature and pressure, not on the mass of the molecules.

questions.stem_md: The number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12, 6.022 × 10²³, is known as the ___ number.
questions.solution_md: The number of atoms in 12 g of carbon-12 is the **Avogadro** number (constant).

questions.stem_md: A gas collected from fermenting waste has a density of 1.96 g L⁻¹ at STP. Taking the molar volume as 22.4 L, find its molar mass in g mol⁻¹, to three significant figures.
questions.solution_md: $M = \rho \times V_\text{m} = 1.96 \times 22.4 = 43.90 \approx 43.9$ g mol⁻¹ (the gas is carbon dioxide).

marking_scheme.step: Mass of 22.4 L = density × molar volume

questions.stem_md: Define the atomic mass unit. Chlorine has an atomic mass of 35.5 u although no chlorine atom has this mass. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: One atomic mass unit is one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Chlorine has two isotopes, chlorine-35 (about 75.8 %) and chlorine-37 (about 24.2 %). The value 35.5 u is the average of their masses weighted by natural abundance, so it is not the mass of any single atom.

questions.solution_md: Definition of u; weighted average of isotopes.

marking_scheme.step: u defined as 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
Weighted average of two isotopes explains 35.5

questions.stem_md: A student pours 3.6 g of water into a flask. Find the number of water molecules and the number of hydrogen atoms in the flask (molar mass of water 18 g mol⁻¹, $N_\text{A} = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$).

answer.model_answer_md: $n = 3.6 / 18 = 0.2$ mol, so molecules $= 0.2 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.20 \times 10^{23}$. Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms, so hydrogen atoms $= 2 \times 1.20 \times 10^{23} = 2.41 \times 10^{23}$.

questions.solution_md: Moles, then molecules, then atoms.

questions.stem_md: A gas jar holds 5.6 L of methane, CH₄, at STP (molar volume 22.4 L, molar mass 16 g mol⁻¹). Calculate (i) the amount of methane in moles, (ii) its mass and (iii) the number of hydrogen atoms present.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $n = 5.6 / 22.4 = 0.25$ mol. (ii) $m = 0.25 \times 16 = 4.0$ g. (iii) Each molecule has 4 hydrogen atoms: $0.25 \times 4 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ atoms.

questions.solution_md: Moles from volume; mass from moles; atoms from moles.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define the mole and state the value of the Avogadro constant. [2]

(b) A sample of anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ (molar mass 106 g mol⁻¹), has a mass of 10.6 g. Calculate (i) the amount in moles, (ii) the number of sodium ions, and (iii) the total number of atoms in the sample. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The mole is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12; the Avogadro constant is $6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. (b) (i) $n = 10.6 / 106 = 0.100$ mol. (ii) Each formula unit gives 2 sodium ions: $2 \times 0.100 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.20 \times 10^{23}$. (iii) Each formula unit has $2 + 1 + 3 = 6$ atoms: $6 \times 0.100 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.61 \times 10^{23}$.

questions.solution_md: Definition; moles; ions; atoms.

questions.stem_md: An unlabelled white powder from a chemical store is analysed and found to contain 43.4 % sodium, 11.3 % carbon and 45.3 % oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is:
questions.solution_md: In 100 g: Na $= 43.4/23 = 1.89$ mol, C $= 11.3/12 = 0.94$ mol, O $= 45.3/16 = 2.83$ mol. Dividing by the smallest (0.94) gives $2.00 : 1 : 3.01 \approx 2 : 1 : 3$, so the formula is $\ce{Na2CO3}$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The fertiliser urea has the formula $\ce{CO(NH2)2}$. Its percentage of nitrogen by mass is:
questions.solution_md: Molar mass $= 12 + 16 + 2(14 + 2) = 60$ g mol⁻¹. Two nitrogen atoms contribute 28 g, so $\%\ \text{N} = 28 / 60 \times 100 = 46.7$ % — option (c). (a) counts one nitrogen atom only.

questions.stem_md: A compound found in sour milk has the empirical formula CH₂O and a molar mass of 90 g mol⁻¹. Its molecular formula is:
questions.solution_md: Empirical formula mass $= 12 + 2 + 16 = 30$. $n = 90 / 30 = 3$, so the molecular formula is $(\ce{CH2O})_3 = \ce{C3H6O3}$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student compares molecular formulae from a hydrocarbon data sheet. In which pair do the two compounds reduce to one and the same empirical formula?
questions.solution_md: Ethene and propene both reduce to CH₂ — option (a). Methane and ethane reduce to CH₄ and CH₃; ethyne and ethene to CH and CH₂; benzene and cyclohexane to CH and CH₂.

questions.stem_md: Blue vitriol is $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ (Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1). Its percentage of water of crystallisation by mass is:
questions.solution_md: Molar mass $= 159.5 + 5 \times 18 = 249.5$ g mol⁻¹. Water $= 90$ g, so $\% = 90 / 249.5 \times 100 = 36.1$ % — option (b). (a) uses one water molecule, (c) divides by the anhydrous mass.

questions.stem_md: Calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂, is the mineral part of bone (Ca = 40, P = 31, O = 16). Find its percentage of calcium by mass, to three significant figures.
questions.solution_md: Molar mass $= 3 \times 40 + 2(31 + 64) = 310$ g mol⁻¹; calcium $= 120$ g, so $\% = 120 / 310 \times 100 = 38.71 \approx 38.7$ %.

questions.stem_md: A rust-coloured oxide of iron obtained from a mine contains 69.9 % iron and 30.1 % oxygen by mass (Fe = 56, O = 16). Find its empirical formula.

answer.model_answer_md: In 100 g: Fe $= 69.9/56 = 1.248$ mol and O $= 30.1/16 = 1.881$ mol. Dividing by the smaller: Fe : O $= 1 : 1.51$. The ratio 1 : 1.5 is multiplied by 2 to give whole numbers, 2 : 3. The empirical formula is $\ce{Fe2O3}$.

questions.solution_md: Moles, ratio 1 : 1.5, multiply by 2.

marking_scheme.step: Moles of Fe and O, ratio 1 : 1.5

questions.stem_md: A gaseous hydrocarbon from natural gas contains 80.0 % carbon and 20.0 % hydrogen by mass. Its vapour density is 15. Find (i) its empirical formula, (ii) its molar mass and (iii) its molecular formula.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) In 100 g: C $= 80/12 = 6.67$ mol, H $= 20/1 = 20.0$ mol; ratio $1 : 3$, so the empirical formula is $\ce{CH3}$ (mass 15). (ii) Molar mass $= 2 \times \text{vapour density} = 2 \times 15 = 30$ g mol⁻¹. (iii) $n = 30/15 = 2$, so the molecular formula is $\ce{C2H6}$.

questions.solution_md: Empirical CH3; M = 2 × VD = 30; molecular C2H6.

questions.stem_md: A 2.50 g crystal of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated until all the water is driven off, leaving 1.6 g of anhydrous salt (CuSO₄ = 159.5 g mol⁻¹, H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹). Calculate the value of x.
questions.solution_md: Moles of water divided by moles of CuSO4.

questions.stem_md:
A fragrant liquid used as a solvent contains 54.5 % carbon, 9.1 % hydrogen and 36.4 % oxygen by mass. Its molar mass is 88 g mol⁻¹.

(a) Calculate its empirical formula. [3]

(b) Find its molecular formula. [1]

(c) Calculate the mass of oxygen in 4.40 g of the liquid. [1]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) In 100 g: C $= 54.5/12 = 4.54$ mol, H $= 9.1/1 = 9.1$ mol, O $= 36.4/16 = 2.27$ mol. Dividing by the smallest (2.27): $2.00 : 4.00 : 1 \approx 2 : 4 : 1$, so the empirical formula is $\ce{C2H4O}$ (mass 44). (b) $n = 88/44 = 2$, so the molecular formula is $\ce{C4H8O2}$. (c) Mass of oxygen $= 4.40 \times 36.4/100 = 1.60$ g.

questions.solution_md: Moles, ratio 2 : 4 : 1; n = 2; mass fraction.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Moles of C, H and O

questions.stem_md: Phosphoric acid (molar mass 98 g mol⁻¹) is completely neutralised by sodium hydroxide: $\ce{H3PO4 + 3NaOH -> Na3PO4 + 3H2O}$. Its equivalent weight in this reaction is:
questions.solution_md: All three replaceable hydrogen atoms react, so the n-factor (basicity used) is 3 and $E = M/n = 98/3 = 32.7$ g eq⁻¹ — option (b). (c) would apply if only two hydrogens were replaced.

questions.stem_md: Lime water is a solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂ (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1). The equivalent weight of calcium hydroxide as a base is:
questions.solution_md: Molar mass $= 40 + 2 \times 17 = 74$ g mol⁻¹. Calcium hydroxide is diacidic (two OH⁻ per formula unit), so $E = 74/2 = 37$ g eq⁻¹ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The equivalent weight of the salt aluminium sulfate, $\ce{Al2(SO4)3}$ (Al = 27, S = 32, O = 16), is:
questions.solution_md: Molar mass $= 54 + 3 \times 96 = 342$ g mol⁻¹. The total positive charge is $2 \times 3 = 6$, so $E = 342/6 = 57$ g eq⁻¹ — option (c). (a) uses 3, the valency of aluminium only.

questions.stem_md: In acidic solution the dichromate ion, $\ce{Cr2O7^2-}$, is reduced to two chromium(III) ions, so each ion gains 6 electrons. The equivalent weight of potassium dichromate, $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ (K = 39, Cr = 52, O = 16), as an oxidising agent is:
questions.solution_md: Molar mass $= 78 + 104 + 112 = 294$ g mol⁻¹. For an oxidising agent $E = M/(\text{electrons gained per formula unit}) = 294/6 = 49.0$ g eq⁻¹ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Potassium permanganate, KMnO₄, is reduced to Mn²⁺ (5 electrons gained) in acidic solution and to MnO₂ (3 electrons gained) in neutral solution. The ratio of its equivalent weight in acidic solution to that in neutral solution is:
questions.solution_md: $E = M/n$, so $E_\text{acid} : E_\text{neutral} = M/5 : M/3 = 3 : 5$ (numerically $31.6 : 52.7$) — option (d). More electrons gained means a smaller equivalent weight.

questions.stem_md: A divalent metal has an equivalent weight of 20.0 g eq⁻¹. Its atomic mass is:
questions.solution_md: Equivalent weight $= \text{atomic mass}/\text{valency}$, so atomic mass $= 20.0 \times 2 = 40.0$ — option (a). The metal is calcium.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The equivalent weight of every acid is equal to half of its molar mass.

**Reason (R):** All acids are dibasic.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are false. The equivalent weight of an acid is its molar mass divided by its basicity (number of replaceable H⁺ in the reaction): hydrochloric acid is monobasic, so its equivalent weight equals its molar mass, and phosphoric acid can be tribasic — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The equivalent weight of potassium permanganate is different in acidic, neutral and alkaline media.

**Reason (R):** Manganese is reduced to different oxidation states (+2, +4 and +6) in these media, so the number of electrons gained per formula unit differs.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true (31.6, 52.7 and 158 g eq⁻¹ respectively). R is true and explains A: E = M/n and n is 5, 3 and 1 because Mn(+7) goes to Mn(+2), Mn(+4) and Mn(+6) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The equivalent weight of an acid is its molar mass divided by its ___.
questions.solution_md: Equivalent weight of an acid = molar mass ÷ **basicity** (the number of replaceable hydrogen ions, the n-factor).

questions.stem_md: A chemist tabulates substances used in neutralisation titrations (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23, S = 32). Pair each substance with its equivalent weight in g eq⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $98/2 = 49.0$; NaOH is monoacidic: $40/1 = 40.0$; $\ce{Na2CO3}$ has total positive charge 2: $106/2 = 53.0$; $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$ is diacidic: $74/2 = 37.0$.

questions.stem_md: Define equivalent weight and gram equivalent weight, and state how the equivalent weight of an acid is related to its molar mass.

answer.model_answer_md: The equivalent weight of a substance is the number of parts by mass of it that combine with, replace or react with 1 part by mass of hydrogen (8 parts of oxygen); expressed in grams it is the gram equivalent weight. For an acid, equivalent weight = molar mass divided by basicity (the number of replaceable hydrogen ions).

questions.solution_md: Definition; E = M ÷ basicity.

marking_scheme.step: Equivalent weight and gram equivalent weight defined

questions.stem_md: Why does potassium permanganate have more than one equivalent weight? Give its equivalent weight in acidic and in alkaline solution (K = 39, Mn = 55, O = 16).

answer.model_answer_md: The equivalent weight of an oxidising agent is $M/n$ with $n$ the electrons gained per formula unit, and $n$ depends on the medium. In acidic solution $\ce{MnO4-}$ is reduced to $\ce{Mn^2+}$ ($n = 5$), so $E = 158/5 = 31.6$ g eq⁻¹. In alkaline solution it is reduced to manganate(VI) ($n = 1$), so $E = 158/1 = 158$ g eq⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: E = M/n with n varying with the medium.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the equivalent weight of (i) barium hydroxide, $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$, (ii) nitric acid, $\ce{HNO3}$, and (iii) iron(II) sulfate, $\ce{FeSO4}$, acting as a reducing agent when $\ce{Fe^2+}$ is oxidised to $\ce{Fe^3+}$ (Ba = 137, Fe = 56, S = 32, N = 14).

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$: $M = 137 + 34 = 171$, acidity 2, so $E = 171/2 = 85.5$ g eq⁻¹. (ii) $\ce{HNO3}$: $M = 63$, basicity 1, so $E = 63$ g eq⁻¹. (iii) $\ce{FeSO4}$: $M = 152$; each Fe²⁺ loses 1 electron, so $E = 152/1 = 152$ g eq⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: E = M/n with n = acidity, basicity, electrons lost.

questions.stem_md: A metal M has an equivalent weight of 20.0 g eq⁻¹ and forms a chloride in which it is divalent (Cl = 35.5). (i) State the relation between equivalent weight, atomic mass and valency. (ii) Find the atomic mass of M. (iii) Find the percentage of chlorine in its chloride.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Equivalent weight $= \text{atomic mass}/\text{valency}$. (ii) Atomic mass $= 20.0 \times 2 = 40.0$. (iii) The chloride is $\ce{MCl2}$ with molar mass $40.0 + 71 = 111.0$ g mol⁻¹, so $\%\ \text{Cl} = 71/111.0 \times 100 = 64.0$ %.

questions.solution_md: A = E × valency; MCl2 composition.

questions.stem_md:
Phosphoric acid (molar mass 98 g mol⁻¹) reacts with sodium hydroxide in three different ways:

(1) $\ce{H3PO4 + NaOH -> NaH2PO4 + H2O}$
(2) $\ce{H3PO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2HPO4 + 2H2O}$
(3) $\ce{H3PO4 + 3NaOH -> Na3PO4 + 3H2O}$

(a) Calculate the equivalent weight of phosphoric acid in each reaction and explain why it is variable. [3]

(b) Find the number of gram equivalents in 9.8 g of phosphoric acid in each reaction. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The equivalent weight is $M/\text{basicity}$, and the basicity is the number of hydrogens replaced in the reaction: (1) $98/1 = 98.0$; (2) $98/2 = 49.0$; (3) $98/3 = 32.7$ g eq⁻¹. It is variable because the same acid can lose one, two or three H⁺ depending on the amount of base. (b) $n = 9.8/98 = 0.10$ mol, so the gram equivalents are $0.10 \times 1 = 0.10$, $0.10 \times 2 = 0.20$ and $0.10 \times 3 = 0.30$.

questions.stem_md: A technician dissolves 4 g of sodium hydroxide (molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹) in 250 g of water to make a cleaning solution. The molality of the solution is:
questions.solution_md: $n = 4/40 = 0.10$ mol; mass of solvent $= 0.250$ kg. Molality $= 0.10/0.250 = 0.40$ mol kg⁻¹ — option (d). (a) divides by 1 kg and (c) uses the mass of the solution.

questions.stem_md: A reagent bottle is prepared by dissolving 9.8 g of phosphoric acid (molar mass 98 g mol⁻¹) in water and making the volume up to 250 mL. The molarity of the solution is:
questions.solution_md: $n = 9.8/98 = 0.100$ mol; $V = 0.250$ L. Molarity $= 0.100/0.250 = 0.40$ mol L⁻¹ — option (c). (a) divides by 1 L instead of 0.250 L.

questions.stem_md: A 0.20 M solution of phosphoric acid is used to prepare sodium phosphate, $\ce{H3PO4 + 3NaOH -> Na3PO4 + 3H2O}$. The normality of the acid solution for this reaction is:
questions.solution_md: Normality $= \text{molarity} \times \text{n-factor} = 0.20 \times 3 = 0.60$ N — option (a). (d) would be the value if only two hydrogens were replaced.

questions.stem_md: A disinfectant is made by mixing 23 g of ethanol (molar mass 46 g mol⁻¹) with 36 g of water (molar mass 18 g mol⁻¹). The mole fraction of ethanol in the mixture is:
questions.solution_md: $n(\text{ethanol}) = 23/46 = 0.5$ mol; $n(\text{water}) = 36/18 = 2.0$ mol. $x = 0.5/(0.5 + 2.0) = 0.20$ — option (c). (d) is the mole fraction of water.

questions.stem_md: A laboratory attendant has concentrated hydrochloric acid of molarity 12.0 M. The volume of it needed to prepare 250 mL of 0.600 M acid is:

**Assertion (A):** The normality of a 0.10 M solution of sulfuric acid is 0.20 N.

**Reason (R):** Sulfuric acid is a strong acid.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: normality = molarity × n-factor = 0.10 × 2 = 0.20 N. R is also true, but the strength of an acid has nothing to do with the n-factor; the factor 2 comes from the two replaceable hydrogen ions — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The molality of a solution changes when the temperature is changed, because the volume of the solution changes.
questions.solution_md: False. Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Mass does not change with temperature, so molality is temperature independent; it is molarity (which uses volume) that changes.

questions.stem_md: A chemistry notebook lists concentration terms and their definitions in a jumbled order. Pair each term with its definition.

match_right.text_md: moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
moles of one component divided by total moles of all components
gram equivalents of solute per litre of solution
moles of solute per litre of solution

questions.solution_md: Molarity uses litres of solution; molality uses kilograms of solvent; normality uses gram equivalents per litre of solution; mole fraction is a ratio of moles.

questions.stem_md: A bottle of liquid soap contains 4 g of sodium hydroxide dissolved in 250 mL of solution (molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹, equivalent weight 40 g eq⁻¹). Express its concentration as percent w/v and as molarity.

answer.model_answer_md: Percent w/v $= 4/250 \times 100 = 1.6$ %. Moles $= 4/40 = 0.100$ mol in 0.250 L, so molarity $= 0.100/0.250 = 0.40$ M (and since the n-factor is 1, the normality is also 0.40 N).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define molality and normality. State, with a reason, which of molarity and molality is independent of temperature. [2]

(b) A bottle of concentrated hydrochloric acid is labelled "36.5 % w/w, density 1.18 g mL⁻¹" (molar mass of HCl 36.5 g mol⁻¹; water 18 g mol⁻¹). For this acid calculate (i) the molarity, (ii) the molality and (iii) the mole fraction of HCl. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Molality is the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; normality is the number of gram equivalents of solute per litre of solution. Molality is temperature independent because masses do not change with temperature, whereas molarity depends on volume, which changes. (b) Take 100 g of acid: 36.5 g HCl is 1.00 mol and 63.5 g is water. (i) Volume $= 100/1.18 = 84.7$ mL, so molarity $= 1.00/0.0847 = 11.8$ M (equivalently $10 \times 36.5 \times 1.18 / 36.5 = 11.8$). (ii) Molality $= 1.00/0.0635 = 15.75$ mol kg⁻¹. (iii) $n(\ce{H2O}) = 63.5/18 = 3.53$ mol, so $x = 1.00/(1.00 + 3.53) = 0.221$.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; take 100 g of solution; molarity, molality, mole fraction.

questions.stem_md:
A student dissolves 1.325 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate (equivalent weight 53 g eq⁻¹) in water and makes the volume up to 250 mL.

(a) Calculate the normality and the molarity of the sodium carbonate solution. [2]

(b) 25.0 mL of this solution requires 20.8 mL of dilute hydrochloric acid for complete neutralisation (methyl orange indicator). Find the normality and the strength in g L⁻¹ of the acid (HCl = 36.5). [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Gram equivalents $= 1.325/53 = 0.025$, so $N = 0.025/0.250 = 0.100$ N; the n-factor of sodium carbonate is 2, so $M = 0.100/2 = 0.0500$ M. (b) $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$: $N_\text{acid} = 0.100 \times 25 / 20.8 = 0.1202$ N. For HCl the n-factor is 1, so the molarity is 0.1202 M and the strength is $0.1202 \times 36.5 = 4.39$ g L⁻¹.

questions.solution_md: N = geq/V; N1V1 = N2V2; strength = N × E.

questions.stem_md: Zinc granules react with dilute hydrochloric acid: $\ce{Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2}$. The mass of zinc (Zn = 65) needed to liberate 4.48 L of hydrogen at STP (molar volume 22.4 L) is:
questions.solution_md: $n(\ce{H2}) = 4.48/22.4 = 0.20$ mol. The equation gives 1 mol Zn per mol $\ce{H2}$, so $n(\ce{Zn}) = 0.20$ mol and $m = 0.20 \times 65 = 13.0$ g — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the first step of nitric acid manufacture, $\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}$, a pilot reactor is charged with 3.4 g of ammonia and 4.0 g of oxygen (N = 14, O = 16, H = 1). The limiting reagent and the mass of nitrogen monoxide formed are:
questions.solution_md: $n(\ce{NH3}) = 3.4/17 = 0.200$ mol and $n(\ce{O2}) = 4.0/32 = 0.125$ mol. Dividing by the coefficients: ammonia 0.050, oxygen 0.025; oxygen is smaller, so it is limiting. $n(\ce{NO}) = 0.025 \times 4 = 0.10$ mol, mass $= 0.10 \times 30 = 3.0$ g — option (c). (d) would follow from using ammonia.

questions.stem_md: A lime kiln decomposes limestone: $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$ (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16). The mass of quicklime, CaO, obtained from 25 g of pure calcium carbonate is:
questions.solution_md: $n(\ce{CaCO3}) = 25/100 = 0.25$ mol, which gives 0.25 mol of CaO; $m = 0.25 \times 56 = 14.0$ g — option (a). (c) is the mass of carbon dioxide formed.

questions.stem_md: A camping stove burns butane: $\ce{2C4H10 + 13O2 -> 8CO2 + 10H2O}$. At STP, 2.8 L of butane vapour requires what volume of oxygen at STP for complete combustion?
questions.solution_md: At the same temperature and pressure, volumes are in the ratio of coefficients: $V(\ce{O2}) = 2.8 \times 13/2 = 18.2$ L — option (b). (a) assumes equal volumes, (c) multiplies by 13 instead of 13/2 and (d) is five times the volume of butane.

questions.stem_md: 4.8 g of magnesium ribbon (Mg = 24) is added to a flask containing 9.13 g of hydrogen chloride in solution (HCl = 36.5): $\ce{Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2}$. The mass of magnesium left unreacted is:
questions.solution_md: $n(\ce{Mg}) = 4.8/24 = 0.20$ mol and $n(\ce{HCl}) = 9.13/36.5 = 0.25$ mol, which needs only 0.125 mol of Mg. HCl is limiting, and Mg left $= (0.20 - 0.125) \times 24 = 1.8$ g — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The limiting reagent decides the amount of product formed in a reaction.

**Reason (R):** The limiting reagent is the reactant that is present in the smallest mass.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the product stops forming when the limiting reagent is used up. R is false: the limiting reagent is the one with the smallest value of moles divided by its coefficient; a reactant present in a small mass may still be in excess — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In any reaction, the reactant present in the smallest mass is always the limiting reagent.
questions.solution_md: False. The limiting reagent is found from amounts in moles divided by the stoichiometric coefficients, not from masses; a light reactant with a small molar mass may be present in more moles than a heavy one.

questions.stem_md: The reactant that is completely consumed first and so decides the amount of product is called the ___ reagent.
questions.solution_md: It is the **limiting** reagent; the other reactant is in excess.

questions.stem_md: A blacksmith heats 5.6 g of iron (Fe = 56) in excess oxygen: $\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$. Find the mass of iron(III) oxide formed (Fe₂O₃ = 160 g mol⁻¹).
questions.solution_md: $n(\ce{Fe}) = 5.6/56 = 0.10$ mol; from the equation $n(\ce{Fe2O3}) = 0.10 \times 2/4 = 0.05$ mol; $m = 0.05 \times 160 = 8.0$ g.

questions.stem_md: Marble chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid: $\ce{CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2}$. Calculate the mass and the volume at STP of carbon dioxide produced from 10 g of pure calcium carbonate (molar mass 100 g mol⁻¹).

answer.model_answer_md: $n(\ce{CaCO3}) = 10/100 = 0.10$ mol, which gives 0.10 mol of $\ce{CO2}$. Mass $= 0.10 \times 44 = 4.40$ g; volume at STP $= 0.10 \times 22.4 = 2.24$ L.

questions.solution_md: One mole of CaCO3 gives one mole of CO2.

questions.stem_md: In a Haber-process plant, 14 g of nitrogen (molar mass 28 g mol⁻¹) reacts completely with hydrogen: $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$. Find the volume of ammonia formed and the volume of hydrogen consumed, both at STP (molar volume 22.4 L).

answer.model_answer_md: $n(\ce{N2}) = 14/28 = 0.5$ mol. Ammonia: $2 \times 0.5 = 1.0$ mol, so $V = 1.0 \times 22.4 = 22.4$ L. Hydrogen: $3 \times 0.5 = 1.5$ mol, so $V = 33.6$ L.

questions.solution_md: Mole ratio 1 : 3 : 2, then × 22.4 L.

questions.stem_md: 8 g of methane is burnt in 8 g of oxygen in a closed combustion cell: $\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}$ (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16). Find (i) the limiting reagent, (ii) the mass of carbon dioxide formed and (iii) the mass of the excess reagent left over.

answer.model_answer_md: $n(\ce{CH4}) = 8/16 = 0.50$ mol and $n(\ce{O2}) = 8/32 = 0.25$ mol. (i) Moles ÷ coefficient: methane 0.50, oxygen 0.125; oxygen is smaller, so oxygen is the limiting reagent. (ii) $n(\ce{CO2}) = 0.125$ mol, so $m = 0.125 \times 44 = 5.5$ g. (iii) Methane used $= 0.125$ mol, so left $= (0.50 - 0.125) \times 16 = 6.0$ g.

questions.solution_md: Moles ÷ coefficient identifies the limiting reagent.

questions.stem_md: A student wants 6.72 L of oxygen at STP by heating potassium chlorate: $\ce{2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2}$ (KClO₃ = 122.5 g mol⁻¹, KCl = 74.5 g mol⁻¹). Calculate (i) the amount of oxygen needed, (ii) the mass of potassium chlorate to be heated and (iii) the mass of potassium chloride left.
questions.solution_md: Mole ratio 2 : 3 between KClO3 and O2.

questions.stem_md:
A reactor is charged with 28.0 g of nitrogen and 4.0 g of hydrogen (N = 14, H = 1): $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$.

(a) Show by calculation which reactant is the limiting reagent. [2]

(b) Calculate (i) the mass of ammonia formed, (ii) the mass of the excess reagent left, and (iii) the volume of ammonia at STP (molar volume 22.4 L). [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $n(\ce{N2}) = 28/28 = 1.00$ mol; $n(\ce{H2}) = 4/2 = 2.00$ mol. Moles ÷ coefficient: nitrogen 1.00, hydrogen 0.667. Hydrogen is smaller, so hydrogen is the limiting reagent. (b)(i) $n(\ce{NH3}) = 2.00 \times 2/3 = 1.333$ mol, so $m = 1.333 \times 17 = 22.7$ g. (ii) Nitrogen used $= 0.667$ mol, so nitrogen left $= (1.00 - 0.667) \times 28 = 9.33$ g. (iii) $V = 1.333 \times 22.4 = 29.9$ L.

questions.solution_md: Moles ÷ coefficient; hydrogen limiting; yield from hydrogen.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Hydrogen identified as limiting with the comparison
